common_name: Sombrero Adobe Orange Coneflower (Compact Heat-Tolerant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sombrero Adobe Orange is a Proven Winners/Darwin Perennials coneflower bred for compact size, heavy branching, and strong heat and drought tolerance, well suited to a hot Gulf South summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sombrero Adobe Orange is part of the popular Sombrero coneflower series, bred for a compact, sturdy, heavily branched habit that produces far more flowers per plant than older coneflower varieties. The vivid, warm orange, sun-facing blooms hold their color well through summer heat, and the plant's heat and drought tolerance make it a strong performer once established in a Gulf South pollinator or perennial border. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.
sources: Walters Gardens — US Plant Patent PP26639

common_name: Sombrero Salsa Red Coneflower (Compact Hardy Orange-Red Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Salsa Red is a Sombrero-series coneflower bred for improved winter hardiness and branching over earlier coneflower hybrids, giving reliable perennial return in a Gulf South border.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Salsa Red bears single, orange-red flowers on a compact, well-branched plant bred as part of the Sombrero series for improved hardiness and vigor over some earlier coneflower hybrids that struggled to reliably return as perennials. The strong branching habit produces a heavier flush of bloom than older single-stem coneflower types, and the plant tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom through summer, or leave seed heads standing into fall and winter for goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.
sources: Walters Gardens — US Plant Patent PP23105

common_name: Pica Bella Purple Coneflower (Mt. Cuba Top-Performing Compact Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pica Bella was rated a top performer in the Mt. Cuba Center's Echinacea trial for its compact, floriferous habit and strong pollinator appeal.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pica Bella is a purple coneflower selection that earned a top score in the Mt. Cuba Center's rigorous multi-year Echinacea trial, valued for a compact, well-proportioned habit that produces an exceptionally heavy flush of classic purple-pink blooms with a prominent orange-bronze cone. Its strong, reliable flower production makes it a magnet for bees and butterflies through a long summer bloom season. Like other coneflowers it is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond deadheading to prolong bloom. Leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Echinacea for the Mid-Atlantic Region Trial

common_name: Viette's Little Suzy Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Deer-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Viette's Little Suzy was bred by noted Virginia perennial grower André Viette for a notably compact, sturdy habit compared to the popular Goldsturm black-eyed susan.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Viette's Little Suzy is a compact black-eyed susan cultivar, notably shorter and tidier than the widely grown Goldsturm, bred by longtime Virginia perennial nurseryman André Viette for a sturdy, floriferous plant that fits into smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings. It produces the familiar golden-yellow, dark-centered daisy flowers over a long summer bloom season, drawing bees and butterflies while resisting deer and drought once established. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display tidy and encourage continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter for goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Golden Gain Threadleaf Coreopsis (Larger-Flowered Zagreb Improvement)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Golden Gain is a threadleaf coreopsis cultivar bred for larger, more richly golden flowers than the classic Zagreb selection, on a dense, compact clump of fine, lacy foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Golden Gain bears larger, more vividly golden-yellow flowers than the older Zagreb threadleaf coreopsis, held above a dense, tidy clump of fine, needle-like foliage that gives the plant an airy, fine-textured look even out of bloom. It flowers heavily from early summer into fall, drawing bees and small pollinators, and tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny Gulf Coast border. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage a fresh round of flowers and keep the habit tidy. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring if the center begins to thin.
